title: Detection of Scan Databases
summary: This detection strategy covers adversary use of public internet scan databases, which continuously map exposed services and publish the results. An attacker queries those datasets to find your internet facing hosts, open ports, software versions and certificates without touching your network at all. The telemetry that makes it visible is honeypot or deception service logging on unused public addresses, firewall deny logs from known scanning ranges, passive domain name system and certificate records, and your own external attack surface inventory. It fails in practice because the query happens on somebody else's platform, so most organisations see only the later active scan or exploitation step.

beginner.definition: A scan database is a public collection of internet scan results. It shows which addresses answer on which ports. Anyone can search it, sometimes for free. An attacker uses it to learn about your exposed systems without sending you any traffic. This detection looks for the traces that remain.
beginner.whyItMatters: Research that never touches your network is very hard to detect. That is the main problem with these datasets. An attacker can learn your software versions and certificate names in silence. Your network sensors record nothing, so your monitoring looks calm. What you can control is your own exposure. If you know what the scan databases show, you can close the service before somebody uses the listing. Deception addresses help, because a service that nobody should find will still be probed.
howItWorks: You place a deception service on a public address that no real system uses.
Internet scanning engines and curious attackers connect to that address, and the service records the attempt.
Your firewall logs also record denied connections from known scanning address ranges.
The detection enriches each attempt with ownership data and with your exposure inventory.
An attempt against an address that should be silent is a strong indicator of a scan database listing.
The rule alerts with the address, the port and the first time that address was contacted.
beginner.example: Imagine a street of houses where one house is empty and dark. The owner wants to know who is looking at it. So he installs a movement sensor behind the front window. Every person who peers in and tries the handle is written into a small log. The neighbours receive deliveries all day, so their doorbells ring constantly and mean nothing. The empty house is different, because nobody has a reason to test its door. Your deception address is that empty house. The sensor log tells you when somebody has been reading a list of targets.
takeaways: Public scan databases let an attacker study you without touching your network.
Unused public addresses are valuable because no honest visitor should find them.
Watching your own exposure is as important as watching inbound traffic.

objectives: Explain what a public internet scan database contains and who uses it.
Describe why deception addresses reveal scan database listings.
Correlate firewall deny events with address ownership information.
Summarise your own exposure using external inventory snapshots.
Prioritise closing services that appear in public scan results.
dataSources: Deception or honeypot service logs on unused public addresses, with source address, port and timestamp
Firewall or edge router deny logs with source address, destination port and rule name
External attack surface inventory snapshots that list your public addresses, open ports and service banners
Certificate transparency and passive domain name system records for your public names
Address ownership enrichment data identifying known internet scanning and hosting ranges
logic: The pattern is contact with a public address that should receive no legitimate traffic, combined with known scanning source ranges that appear in your deny logs. The fields that must be correlated are the destination address, the destination port, the source address and its owning organisation, the first and last time the address was contacted, and whether the address appears in your exposure inventory at all. Benign traffic to unused addresses is rare, but monitoring services and health checks can produce it. The malicious case shows short, repeated connections to many ports on an address that carries no service, which is consistent with a target list taken from a scan database.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Probe Against Unused Public Address From Scanning Range
# logsource:
#   product: network
# detection:
#   selection:
#     action: 'deny'
#     dst_ip|in: 'unused_public_addresses'
#   filter_monitoring:
#     src_ip|in: 'internal_monitoring_ranges'
#   condition: selection and not filter_monitoring | count(distinct dst_port) by src_ip > 20
# level: low
falsePositives: Internal vulnerability scanners and availability monitors that check a reserved address by mistake.
Internet background noise from worms and botnets that probe every routable address.
Cloud provider health checks that contact addresses you have released but not removed from routing.
Security researchers who scan broad ranges and publish aggregate statistics only.
tuningNotes: Keep the deception address list current, because an address that later becomes a real service turns the rule into noise. Add a filter for your own scanning and monitoring ranges and for cloud provider health check ranges. Scope the rule to addresses that have been unused for more than thirty days. If you narrow it to a short list of addresses you see fewer alerts, but you also lose the broad view of which parts of your range are being enumerated, so keep a separate weekly summary instead of an alert for that.
